[Isaiah 1:16-20] Desiring, therefore, that all His beloved should be partakers of repentance, He has, by His almighty will, established [these declarations].
Clement's First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 8

Come now, you tightrope walker, walking on a tightrope of purity and chastity and every sort of sexual asceticism, you who, on the slender cord of a discipline like this, far from the path of truth, advance with reluctant feet, balancing the flesh by the spirit, moderating your desires by the faith, guarding your eyes through fear, why do you watch your step so anxiously?

Having considered God's generosity, we pray next for his indulgence. For of what benefit is food if, in reality, we are bent on it like a bull on his victim? Our Lord knew that he alone was without sin. Therefore he taught us to say in prayer, "Forgive us our trespasses." A prayer for pardon is an acknowledgment of sin, since one who asks for pardon confesses guilt. Thus, too, repentance is shown to be acceptable to God, because God wills this rather than the death of the sinner.

He who has thus satisfied God, who by repentance for his deed, who by shame for his sin has conceived more of both virtue and faith from the very sorrow for his lapsing, after being heard and aided by the Lord, will cause the church to rejoice, which he recently had saddened, and will merit not only the pardon of God but a crown.

But that it may be made certain for thee that a sinner is called dead even when he lives, I will make it clear to thee. If you have any hope of salvation; if you have the least thought of God, or any desire for good things to come; if you have any fear of the chastisements reserved for the impenitent, awake without delay, lift up your eyes to heaven, come to your senses, cease from your wickedness, shake off the stupor that enwraps you, make a stand against the foe who has struck you down. Make an effort to rise from the ground. Remember the good Shepherd who will follow and rescue you. Though it be but two legs or a lobe of an ear, spring back from the beast that has wounded you. Remember the mercies of God and how He cures with oil and wine. Do not despair of salvation. Recall your recollection of how it is written in the Scriptures that he who is falling rises and he who turns away returns; the wounded is healed, the prey of beasts escapes; he who owns his sin is not rejected. You, I say, who are timid after being shameless, who are bashful after sinning! You who are not ashamed to sin but are ashamed to confess! And yet God is gracious and merciful. Whence then, whence is that Day so full of agony and anguish? A stream of fire is rolling before His face. The books of our deeds are opened. The day itself is burning as an oven, the angels are flying around, and many furnaces are prepared. How then is He good and merciful, and full of lovingkindness to man? Even herein is He merciful, and He shows in these things the greatness of His lovingkindness. For He holds forth to us these terrors, that being constrained by them, we may be awakened to the desire of the kingdom.

Nothing makes God so angry as when people from despair of better things cleave to those which are worse; and indeed this despair in itself is a sign of unbelief. One who despairs of salvation can have no expectation of a judgment to come.

Now therefore, Christians, since we know from the holy Scriptures and from divine revelations how great is the grace that God dispenses to those who truly run to him for refuge and who blot out their sins through repentance, and also how, according to his promise, he rewards them with good things and neither takes vengeance according to what is just nor bring on people a punishment for their sins, let us not be in despair of our lives.

You though, standing there, having made no decision to put yourself right—let me speak like this as though to a single person. Whoever you are, you do not want to put yourself right; what are you promising yourself?

Hear the Scripture: “I will not the death of a sinner, but rather that he should turn, and live.” By these words of God, he is brought back to hope; but there is another snare to be feared, lest through this very hope he sin the more. What then didst thou also say, thou who through hope sinnest yet more? “Whensoever I turn, God will forgive me all; I will do whatsoever I will.” Say not then, “To-morrow I will turn, to-morrow I will please God; and all to-day’s and yesterday’s deeds shall be forgiven me.” Thou sayest true: God hath promised pardon to thy conversion; He hath not promised a to-morrow to thy delay.

For the purpose of God whereby He made man not to perish but to live for ever, stands immovable. And when His goodness sees in us even the very smallest spark of good will shining forth, which He Himself has struck as it were out of the hard flints of our hearts, He fans and fosters it and nurses it with His breath, as He "willeth all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth," for as He says, "it is not the will of your Father which is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish," and again it says: "Neither will God have a soul to perish, but recalleth," meaning that he that is cast off should not altogether perish. For He is true, and lieth not when He lays down with an oath: "As I live, saith the Lord God, for I will not the death of a sinner, but that he should turn from his way and live." For if He willeth not that one of His little ones should perish, how can we imagine without grievous blasphemy that He does not generally will all men, but only some instead of all to be saved? Those then who perish, perish against His will, as He testifies against each one of them day by day: "Turn from your evil ways, and why will ye die, O house of Israel?" And again: "How often would I have gathered thy children together as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not;" and: "Wherefore is this people in Jerusalem turned away with a stubborn revolting? He wished that Adam's transgression had not occurred. And because God knew beforehand the transgression, he commanded him beforehand not to eat of the fruit of the tree. And because he did not submit to the order, justly he was punished.

As a result, dearly beloved, it was necessary (by the designs of a secret plan) for the unchangeable God (whose will cannot be separated from his goodness) to complete by a deeper mystery the first intentions of his love. It was necessary that human beings, tricked into sin by the devil's wickedness, should not perish in opposition to God's plan.
At whatever age a person will do true penance for his sins and change his life for the better under the illumination of God, he will not be deprived of the gift of forgiveness.

For this reason the Lord descended so that he might save sinners, raise up the dead and bring new life to those wounded by death and to enlighten those who lay in darkness. The Lord truly came and called us to be God's adopted children, to enter into a holy city, ever at peace, to possess a life that will endure forever, to share an incorruptible glory. Let us each strive to come to a good end after a good beginning. Let us persevere in poverty, in our pilgrimage, living in affliction and petitions to God without any shame as we continuously knock at the door.

Let your charity believe devoutly and firmly that God never abandons a person unless he is first deserted by him. Although a person may have committed serious sins once, twice and a third time, God still looks for him.
We must prepare our hearts and bodies for the battle of holy obedience to his instructions. What is not possible to us by nature, let us ask the Lord to supply by the help of his grace.

Let us consider the grace of merciful God, and let us condemn the multitude of our own guilt. Behold, he sees sinners and endures them, tolerates those who resist, and yet daily calls them mercifully through the Gospel. He desires our confession from a pure heart, and has forgiven all that we have done wrong. The mercy of the Redeemer has tempered for us the severity of the law. For in it was written: If anyone does this or that, let him surely die. If anyone does these or those things, let him be overwhelmed with stones. Our Creator and Redeemer appeared in the flesh, promising not punishment but life to the confession of sinners; he receives the woman confessing her wounds, and sends her away healed. He bent the hardness of the law toward mercy, because those whom the law justly condemns, he himself mercifully frees. Hence it is also well written in the law that the hands of Moses were heavy; therefore taking a stone, they placed it underneath, upon which he sat; and Aaron and Hur supported his hands. Moses indeed sat upon a stone, when the law rested upon the Church. But this same law had heavy hands, because it did not mercifully bear with sinners, but struck them with severe punishment. Aaron means mountain of strength, and Hur means fire. Whom therefore does this mountain of strength signify, if not our Redeemer, of whom it is said through the prophet: "In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains"? Or who is figured by fire, if not the Holy Spirit, of whom the same Redeemer says: "I came to cast fire upon the earth"? Therefore Aaron and Hur support the heavy hands of Moses, and by supporting them render them lighter, because the Mediator of God and men, coming with the fire of the Holy Spirit, showed us through spiritual understanding that the heavy commandments of the law, which could not be borne while held carnally, are tolerable for us. For he rendered the hands of Moses light, as it were, because he turned the weight of the law's commandments to the power of confession. He indicated this promise of mercy for us who follow, when he says through the prophet: "I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live." Hence again under the figure of Judea it is said to every sinful soul: "If a man puts away his wife, and she departs and marries another man, will he return to her again? Will not that woman be polluted and contaminated? But you have fornicated with many lovers; nevertheless return to me, says the Lord." Behold, he gave the example of a shameful woman. He showed that after such shame she cannot be received back. But he overcomes by mercy this very example that he set forth, when he says that a fornicating woman can by no means be received back, and yet he himself waits to receive the fornicating soul. Consider, brothers, the weight of such great tenderness. He says what cannot be done, and demonstrates that he himself can do this even against custom. Behold, he calls, and those whom he declares to be defiled, he also seeks to embrace, those by whom he complains he has been abandoned. Let no one therefore waste the time of such great mercy, let no one cast away the offered remedies of divine tenderness.

For the wickedness of the wicked shall not hurt him in the day that he turns from his wickedness. If he acts righteously and walks in the statutes of life, he shall surely live; he shall not die. None of his sins that he committed shall be remembered against him. Because he has made the decree of righteousness, he shall live by it.

And why do you pick out for yourselves the obscure passages of inspired Scripture and then tear them out of context and twist them in order to accomplish your own destruction? Do you not hear Him Who says: "Repent, for the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand" [Matthew 3:2]; and again: "Just so, I tell you, there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents" [Luke 15:7, adapted]? Come, He says, all you who are burdened with many sins, to the One Who takes away the sin of the world; come all who thirst to the fountain which flows and never dies. - "Second Ethical Discourse"

The mediæval mind turned centrally upon the pivot of Free Will. In their social system the mediævals were too much PARTI-PER-PALE, as their heralds would say, too rigidly cut up by fences and quarterings of guild or degree. But in their moral philosophy they always thought of man as standing free and doubtful at the cross-roads in a forest. While they clad and bound the body and (to some extent) the mind too stiffly and quaintly for our taste, they had a much stronger sense than we have of the freedom of the soul. For them the soul always hung poised like an eagle in the heavens of liberty. Many of the things that strike a modern as most fantastic came from their keen sense of the power of choice.

For instance, the greatest of the Schoolmen devotes folios to the minute description of what the world would have been like if Adam had refused the apple; what kings, laws, babies, animals, planets would have been in an unfallen world. So intensely does he feel that Adam might have decided the other way that he sees a complete and complex vision of another world, a world that now can never be.

This sense of the stream of life in a man that may turn either way can be felt through all their popular ethics in legend, chronicle, and ballad. It is a feeling which has been weakened among us by two heavy intellectual forces. The Calvinism of the seventeenth century and the physical science of the nineteenth, whatever other truths they may have taught, have darkened this liberty with a sense of doom. We think of bad men as something like black men, a separate and incurable kind of people. The Byronic spirit was really a sort of operatic Calvinism. It brought the villain upon the stage; the lost soul; the modern version of King John. But the contemporaries of King John did not feel like that about him, even when they detested him. They instinctively felt him to be a man of mixed passions like themselves, who was allowing his evil passions to have much too good a time of it. They might have spoken of him as a man in considerable danger of going to hell; but they would have not talked of him as if he had come from there. In the ballads of Percy or Robin Hood it frequently happens that the King comes upon the scene, and his ultimate decision makes the climax of the tale. But we do not feel, as we do in the Byronic or modern romance, that there is a definite stage direction "Enter Tyrant." Nor do we behold a deus ex machina who is certain to do all that is mild and just. The King in the ballad is in a state of virile indecision. Sometimes he will pass from a towering passion to the most sweeping magnanimity and friendliness; sometimes he will begin an act of vengeance and be turned from it by a jest. Yet this august levity is not moral indifference; it is moral freedom. It is the strong sense in the writer that the King, being the type of man with power, will probably sometimes use it badly and sometimes well. In this sense John is certainly misrepresented, for he is pictured as something that none of his own friends or enemies saw. In that sense he was certainly not so black as he is painted, for he lived in a world where every one was piebald.

King John would be represented in a modern play or novel as a kind of degenerate; a shifty-eyed moral maniac with a twist in his soul's backbone and green blood in his veins. The mediævals were quite capable of boiling him in melted lead, but they would have been quite incapable of despairing of his soul in the modern fashion. A striking a fortiori case is that of the strange mediæval legend of Robert the Devil. Robert was represented as a monstrous birth sent to an embittered woman actually in answer to prayers to Satan, and his earlier actions are simply those of the infernal fire let loose upon earth. Yet though he can be called almost literally a child of hell, yet the climax of the story is his repentance at Rome and his great reparation. That is the paradox of mediæval morals: as it must appear to the moderns. We must try to conceive a race of men who hated John, and sought his blood, and believed every abomination about him, who would have been quite capable of assassinating or torturing him in the extremity of their anger. And yet we must admit that they would not really have been fundamentally surprised if he had shaved his head in humiliation, given all his goods to the poor, embraced the lepers in a lazar-house, and been canonised as a saint in heaven. So strongly did they hold that the pivot of Will should turn freely, which now is rusted, and sticks.

For we, whatever our political opinions, certainly never think of our public men like that. If we hold the opinion that Mr. Lloyd George is a noble tribune of the populace and protector of the poor, we do not admit that he can ever have paltered with the truth or bargained with the powerful. If we hold the equally idiotic opinion that he is a red and rabid Socialist, maddening mobs into mutiny and theft, then we expect him to go on maddening them--and us. We do not expect him, let us say, suddenly to go into a monastery. We have lost the idea of repentance; especially in public things; that is why we cannot really get rid of our great national abuses of economic tyranny and aristocratic avarice. Progress in the modern sense is a very dismal drudge; and mostly consists of being moved on by the police. We move on because we are not allowed to move back. But the really ragged prophets, the real revolutionists who held high language in the palaces of kings, they did not confine themselves to saying, "Onward, Christian soldiers," still less, "Onward, Futurist soldiers"; what they said to high emperors and to whole empires was, "Turn ye, turn ye, why will ye die?"
A Miscellany of Men, The Mediæval Villain (1912)

The heart of the true Middle Ages might be found far better, for instance, in the noble tale of Tannhauser, in which the dead staff broke into leaf and flower to rebuke the pontiff who had declared even one human being beyond the strength of sorrow and pardon.
Alarms and Discursions, A Drama of Dolls (1910)
We must press on and persevere in the faith and virtue and in the consummation of heavenly and spiritual grace, that we may be able to arrive at the palm and the crown.

And from the particular admonition with which he was speaking to the house of Israel, he passes to a general discussion: that past acts of righteousness do not save the righteous man if he has become taken up with new crimes, and old sins do not destroy the sinner or the wicked if he has amended his old errors by works of righteousness, and that God in both cases judges not past things but present ones: 'If I say,' he says, 'to the righteous: You shall live by life, and promise him the rewards of righteousness, and he, trusting in this, sins, all his former righteous deeds will be consigned to oblivion and he will die in his present iniquity; nor has my sentence changed, since I cannot render to the same man, now a sinner, what I had promised to the righteous man; on the contrary, if I threaten the sinner and the wicked — and say: Yet three days and Nineveh shall be overthrown —, and he repents and amends his old error by good works, so that he does judgment and righteousness, restores the pledge, and gives back what he has robbed, walks in the commandments of life, and does nothing unjust: ought he not to live by life, which is Christ, and by no means die, since the threat made to the sinner ought not to punish the righteous man?' — something of the kind the divine word says to Jeremiah when he goes down into the potter's house and hears that God's promises or threat aim at this: either to call men forth to salvation or to deter them from sin — 'hence those who say: The way of the Lord is not fair, are convicted of this, that it is their own judgment that is unfair, since they have a most evil eye and judge by no means the new things but the old'. By all these things it is shown that neither ought the sinner to despair of salvation if he repents, nor the righteous to trust in his righteousness if he has carelessly lost what he had acquired with great labor. We pass quickly over what is plain, in order to linger over what is more obscure; but in what points the present prophecy differs from the earlier one, and in what it says similar things, a comparison of the two will be able to show. Moreover, what it is to do judgment and righteousness, to restore the pledge, to give back what was robbed, to walk in the commandments of life, and the rest, we have said above in this same prophet.
In the lives of Christians we look not to the beginnings but to the endings. Paul began badly but ended well. The start of Judas wins praise; his end is condemned because of his treachery.

For what does it profit a man to be in continence for twenty years, and afterwards to fall? — according to what is written in the prophet: 'The justice of the just man shall not profit him on whatever day he goes astray: it shall not free him, nor save him. And the sin of the sinner shall not harm him on whatever day he turns and does penance.' Neither ought the just man to be secure, nor ought the sinner to despair of his salvation: for in both of them there is both fear and hope.

But behold, while we search out the secrets of the heavenly citizens, we have digressed far from the order of our exposition. Let us therefore sigh toward those of whom we speak, but let us return to ourselves. For we ought to remember that we are flesh. Let us be silent meanwhile about the secrets of heaven, but before the eyes of our Creator let us wipe away the stains of our dust with the hand of repentance. Behold, divine mercy itself promises, saying: There shall be joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance; and yet through the prophet the Lord says: In whatever day the just man shall sin, all his righteousnesses shall be in oblivion before me. Let us consider, if we can, the dispensation of heavenly loving-kindness. To those who stand, if they should fall, he threatens punishment; but to the fallen, that they might desire to rise, he promises mercy. He terrifies those, lest they presume upon their good works; he comforts these, lest they despair in their evils. You are just—fear wrath, lest you fall; you are a sinner—trust in mercy, that you may rise.

If you are righteous, fear his wrath lest you slip; if you are a sinner, believe in his mercy so that you can arise. But see, we have already fallen, we are not strong enough to stand, we lie prostrate in our evil desires. He who created us to be upright still waits, and he appeals to us to rise. He opens up his heart of love and seeks to get us back to himself again through repentance.

Be ye not afraid, O penitents, lest the hope which is written in the Scriptures be cut off; for it is fitting for the Spirit of God thus to warn, for a fearful warning is set in Ezekiel the prophet when He said to him: "If all his days a man shall do judgment and righteousness, and at the end of his days he shall do iniquity, in his iniquity he shall die. And if a man shall do iniquity all his days, and he shall repent and do judgment and righteousness, his soul shall live" (Ezek. 33: 18-19). By this one word He has warned the righteous that he should not sin and lose his course; and He gave hope to the wicked that he should turn from his iniquity and live.

And by Ezekiel He says: When the wicked turns from his way unto the Lord and do that which is lawful and right, the sins he has committed will not be remembered but he shall live, sayeth the Lord. Thus it is also with the righteous; when he turneth from his righteousness and comitteth sin and iniquity, the righteousness he has done will not be remembered but I will lay a stumbling block before him and by the iniquity he has done he shall die if he remains steadfast in it. Why is this? Because the iniquitous will not stumble on account of his iniquity after he turns unto the Lord. But the righteousness of the righteous will not save him when he sins, if he builds his building on that foundation.

This is according to the letter; but according to the ἀναγωγὴν [anagogy, the higher sense]: if 'Hiezechiel' [Ezekiel] means 'strength of God' — and Christ, moreover, is the power of God and the wisdom of God! —, this is to be understood: that, Jerusalem having been taken and overthrown, whoever has been able to escape the faithlessness of the Jews — such as were the apostles and the remnant that was saved —, he himself announces to Christ that all the ceremonies of the Jews have been overthrown — which certain people think must be observed even to this day, not hearing that saying of the Apostle: You have fallen from grace, you who are justified in the law. And I marvel at the obstinacy of men in wishing to defend in word what they do not dare to fulfill in deed, unless perhaps Jewish wolves are hiding under the skin of sheep, that is, of Christians. Why does a defender of the Synagogue make his voice resound in the churches of Christ? —. Jerusalem, therefore, having been taken and overthrown, the mouth of the Lord is opened through the apostles and apostolic men — who can say: My mouth is opened to you, O Corinthians, and: A great and effective door has been opened to me, and that saying: I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit —, a mouth which will never be able to keep silent, nor to hear — along with Israel: Hear, Israel, and be silent —, but will resound in the whole world and will lay open the Gospel of Christ to the nations. Hence, according to this sense, the 'twelfth year' refers to the twelve tribes, and the 'tenth month' to the time of the Jewish propitiation, which in Greek is called ἱλασμὸς, and the 'fifth day of the month' to the fleshly senses — all of which, Jerusalem having been taken and the Gospel succeeding, we have shown to have been abolished and to have passed away —, and 'in the evening', that is, at the consummation of the world, to the hand of the Lord having come upon the true Ezekiel, who had sung of the future ruins of the city through the prophets and in the morning showed that they had been fulfilled.

And it came to pass in the twelfth year, in the tenth month, on the fifth of the month of our exile (or captivity), there came to me one who had fled (or who had been saved) from Jerusalem, saying: The city has been laid waste (or taken). Now the hand of the Lord had come upon me in the evening, before he who had fled came; and he opened my mouth until he came to me in the morning, and, my mouth being opened, I was silent no longer. In the eleventh year of the reign of Zedekiah, in the fifth month, the city of Jerusalem was taken. But this prophecy is dated the twelfth year, the tenth month, the fifth of the month, of the captivity or exile, when he was taken captive with Jeconiah. From this it is shown that one year, four months and twenty-five days after Jerusalem was taken, one of the citizens of Jerusalem came to Babylon to report that the city had been taken and laid waste.

One day before the one who was to tell these things came, in the evening the hand of the Lord came upon the prophet Ezekiel, and it opened his mouth, which had long been closed; and whatever that man was going to say, this one recounted beforehand as already done, and he was silent no longer, seeing his prophecy fulfilled in deed, and that the people who were in Babylon, or those who were captives, by no means doubted the prophetic oracle; for the mouth of the prophet is opened at the moment when he has shown accomplished in deed what he had announced before; and he proclaims with all freedom who points out not future things at all, but things either present or past.

Jerusalem having been taken, as we have said, and the temple overthrown, the poor of the land, of whom Jeremiah writes, had alone been left in Jerusalem, to tend the vineyards and the fields and to dwell in the ruins of the burned city; and though they ought to have repented over the things on account of which the captivity had come, deceiving themselves with an empty hope, they said: 'Our father Abraham was one, and yet he possessed this land by inheritance — not that he himself possessed it, but that his seed received the land of promise; if therefore that one man was multiplied into such great peoples, we, who are many more, who have been left in the land of Judea and dwell in deserted and ruined cities, shall surely be multiplied much more, so that we, being many, may possess what that one man possessed'.

Now let us come to the tropology and, according to our custom, draw the broad discussion together rather than spread it out. Every heretic dwells among crumbling walls and in deserts, and thinks that he possesses the land of Israel: 'If Abraham, one man, by his faith came to such great blessedness that his seed was multiplied like the sand of the sea and like the stars of heaven, how much more shall we, being many, possess the land of 'Israel', that is, 'of those who see God', and 'Iudaea' [Judea], 'of the Lord's confession'?'; to them the Lord answered: 'He possessed the land by the merit of faith; but your unbelief, or rather blasphemy, will not be able to possess the land of Israel, that is, the Church.

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, those who dwell in these ruins upon the soil of Israel speak, saying: Abraham was one, and he possessed the land; but we are many, to us the land has been given as a possession. Therefore you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God: You who eat in blood, and lift up your eyes to your uncleannesses, and shed blood, shall you possess the land by inheritance? You have stood upon your swords, you have done abominations, and each of you has defiled his neighbor's wife, and shall you possess the land by inheritance? These things you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God: As I live, those who dwell in the ruins shall fall by the sword, and he who is in the field shall be given to the beasts to be devoured, but those who are in strongholds and in caves shall die of pestilence. And I will give the land into solitude and into desert, and its proud strength shall fail, and the mountains of Israel shall be made desolate, because there is no one who passes through them; and they shall know that I am the Lord, when I have made their land desolate and deserted, because of all their abominations which they have wrought. And you, son of man, the sons of your people talk about you beside the walls and in the doorways of the houses, and they say one to another, a man to his neighbor, speaking: Come, and let us hear what is the word that comes forth from the Lord. And they come to you as if a people were entering (or as a people is accustomed to gather), and my people sit before you; and they hear your words and do not do them, for they turn them into a song of their mouth, and their heart follows its avarice. (or, as is contained in the Seventy, for they make a lie in their mouth, and their heart walks after their abominations. It follows:) And you are to them like a musical song which is sung with a sweet and pleasing sound, and they will hear your words and will not do them. And when what has been foretold comes — for behold, it is coming —, then they will know that you prophesied in their midst. First it must be known that some eight lines, more or less, from the place we have set down: You who eat in blood, and lift up your eyes to your uncleannesses, up to the place where it is written: These things you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God, are not found in the Seventy, who omitted these too along with many others; or else, having been translated by them, they were gradually removed through the fault of copyists. And our Latins, or rather envious Christians, and, to speak more openly, heirs of the Grunnian faction, bark against us: why do we expound according to the Hebrew — as though food were to be forced upon the unwilling, and the banquet were not being prepared for those who receive it with thanksgiving; surely, if they do not trust us, let them read the other editions: of Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion; let them question Hebrews — not of one place, lest they keep boasting that they were bought by me, but of different provinces; and when they see that all agree with my error or inexperience, then let them understand that they are excessively wise, and desire to sleep rather than to learn —, and let them dwell in the seventy little cells of the Alexandrian Pharos, lest they lose the sails from their ships and sigh over the loss of their ropes. So much against the envious; now let us discuss what we have set before us.

To them the Lord answered that Abraham, one man, had possessed the land of promise by faith — For Abraham believed, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness —, but that these, taken up with unbelief and crimes, even if they are more, cannot possess it; and at the same time he enumerates by what deeds they offend God, namely six kinds of sins: 'You who eat in blood, and lift up your eyes to uncleannesses, that is, to your idols, and shed blood, that is, commit homicide; doing these things, will you be able to keep the land by inheritance? Nor are you content with this limit of crimes, but you stand upon your swords daily, ready to kill and imitating Esau, who stood, and lived by his sword; you do incredible abominations, namely the foulnesses of lusts; and each one defiles his neighbor's wife, so that he is the more wicked in this, that he had defiled the wife of a friend and neighbor. Would you do these things,' he says, 'and suppose that you will hold the land by inheritance?

For first, you eat in blood, pouring out the blood of those whom you cause to stumble; next, you lift up your eyes to uncleannesses or to your abominations which you have fabricated out of your own mind — when you ought to have imitated the man of the Church and said: To you I have lifted up my eyes, you who dwell in the heavens —; third, you shed blood, not giving life to those whom you have led astray, but killing them; nor is it enough for you to have done these three things, but you stand upon your swords, that is, you persevere in the depravity of your opinion, and are ready for slaughter; and you have done abominations, doing in bedchambers things that are shameful to speak of; and you have defiled the wife of your neighbor, hastening, namely, to snatch away daily from the embrace of Christ, by deceiving them, those of the Church's way of life. And when you have done these things, do you think that you will hold the land of Israel by inheritance?'

To them God says that whoever has dwelt in the ruined conventicles of the heretics shall fall by the sword of the Church — of which it is written: And two-edged swords in their hands, and in the Gospel: I did not come to send peace, but a sword, and: 'The servant who gives himself over to luxury and leisure shall be divided, that is, shall be struck with the blade, and his portion shall be placed with the unbelievers' —, and he who is in the field, or in the open country, shall be given to the beasts to be devoured — the beasts which the prophet, desiring to avoid them, prays against: Do not give to the beasts the soul that confesses to you —, but he who is in strongholds and in walled places — of which it is written: The righteous man went up against the strongest cities and destroyed their fortifications, in which the wicked trusted — and lingers in caves — of which it is said: It is written: The house of my Father shall be called a house of prayer; but you have made it a den of robbers —, that one shall die by famine of the word of the Lord and by pestilence; and the whole land of the heretics shall be given into solitude, so that their pride may be broken and the mountains which promised themselves the loftiness of knowledge may be reduced to solitude — mountains that are called of Israel because under the name of Christ they trip up all whom they deceive —, and no one shall pass through them — nor will anyone be able to say what Moses said: Passing over, I will see this great vision; for they are inhabitants of the perverse mountains, not pilgrims and sojourners —, so that, when they have suffered these things, they may then know that he himself is the Lord, who has given their land into solitude because of the abominations which they have wrought.

Answer them therefore, O prophet, and bring forth this sentence upon them from my word: I swear by myself that those who dwell in the ruins and the crumbling walls shall fall by the sword, and those who are in the fields — or in the open country — shall be devoured by beasts, and those who are in walled places — or in strongholds — and in caves shall not be able to escape the wrath of God, but shall die by famine and pestilence.

And I will give,' he says, 'the land of Judea into solitude, and its proud strength shall fail — which had once been strength: The proud, however, God resists, and gives grace to the humble —; the mountains too and everything shall be deserted, and they shall come into such solitude that no one passes through them; and then the few who had remained shall by no means trust in their multitude, but shall know, by the greatness of the solitude, that I am the Lord, who gave the land into desert because of all the abominations which they have wrought'. Let these things be said against those who, Jerusalem having been taken and the whole region of the Jews laid waste, dwelt, a few of them, in the ruined and deserted cities and little villages.

There follows — on the same day indeed and at the same time, that is, in the twelfth year, the tenth month, on the fifth of the month, when the one who had fled from Jerusalem came, and when the prophet spoke to those who were in the land of Judea and promised themselves the hope of an everlasting possession — and he commands the prophet to speak to the people that lives in Babylon and dwells with him, and to rebuke them for their flattering snares, those who desire to hear the words of the prophet not for the salvation of the soul but for the pleasure of the ears; these walk beside the walls and in the doorways of the houses, by no means desiring to enter into the prophet's meaning, but they urge one another on and say: Come, and let us hear what is the word that comes forth from the Lord.

'And so they come like a people entering the Church of God, and they sit before you, my people, which says that it is mine, and they are unwilling to do what they have heard; people of this sort seem to me like those who are beguiled by theatrical songs and listen either to tragedians or to comedians and are there caressed with pleasure, so that, when they have gone out from you, they repeat these things and sing them over and deceive themselves with the sweet sound: And they will hear,' he says, 'your words and will not do them'. Such, even to this day, are many in the churches, who say: 'Come, let us hear this man and that man', as he rolls out the words of his preaching with marvelous eloquence; and they stir up applause and shout and wave their hands; and the things they had neglected in deeds, once they learn that these have come — for what the prophet pronounces by the word of God must come —, then they will begin to acknowledge, and to know that all that they had heard were not the words of a man, but of the Lord, who spoke through the prophet and the man of the Church.
34: And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, prophesy concerning the shepherds (or to the shepherds) of Israel, prophesy and say to the shepherds: Thus says the Lord God: Woe to the shepherds of Israel who were feeding themselves (or O shepherds of Israel, do shepherds feed themselves); are not the flocks fed by the shepherds (or do not the shepherds feed the sheep)? You ate the milk and covered yourselves with the wool, and what was fat you slaughtered, but my flock you did not feed; what was weak you did not make firm (or strengthen), and what was sick you did not heal, what was broken you did not bind up, and what was cast off (or was straying) you did not bring back, what had perished you did not seek, but you ruled over them with harshness and with power (or and what was strong, you afflicted with toil). And my sheep were scattered, because there was no shepherd (or shepherds); and they were made to be devoured by all the beasts of the field, and they were scattered. My flocks (or sheep) had wandered over all the mountains and on every high hill, and over the whole face of the earth my flocks (or sheep) were scattered; and there was none who would seek, there was none, I say, who would seek (or who would bring back). Therefore, O shepherds, hear the word of the Lord: As I live, says the Lord God, because my flocks (or sheep) have become a prey, and my sheep have been made to be devoured by all the beasts of the field, because there was no shepherd (or shepherds); for the shepherds did not seek my flock, but the shepherds were feeding themselves, and were not feeding my flocks. Therefore, shepherds, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I myself, against the shepherds, will require my flock at their hand, and I will make them cease, so that they no longer feed my flock, nor shall the shepherds feed themselves any more (or the sheep); and I will deliver my flock (or sheep) from their mouth, and it shall no longer be food for them. For thus says the Lord God: Behold, I myself will seek out my sheep, and I will visit them. As a shepherd visits his flock on the day when he is in the midst of his scattered sheep (or when there is gloom and cloud in the midst of his separated sheep), so will I visit my sheep, and I will deliver them from all the places into which they had been scattered in the day of cloud and gloom. And I will lead them (or them) out from the peoples (or from the nations), and I will gather them (or them) from the lands (or regions), and I will bring them (or them) into their own land, and I will feed them (or them) on the mountains, Israel, by the streams and in all the dwelling places of the land. In the richest pastures I will feed them (or them), and on the high mountains of Israel shall be their pastures (or their folds); there they shall rest in green grass, and in fat pastures they shall feed upon the mountains of Israel. I will feed my sheep, and I will make them lie down (or rest), says the Lord God. What had perished I will seek, and what had been cast off (or had strayed) I will bring back, and what had been broken I will bind up, and what was weak I will make firm (or strengthen), and what is fat and strong I will guard, and I will feed them in judgment (or with judgment). But you, my flocks (or my sheep), thus says the Lord God: Behold, I judge between cattle and cattle, of rams and of he-goats. Was it not enough for you to graze down the good pasture? Moreover you will also trample the remnants of your pastures with your feet, and when you drank the purest water, you fouled the rest with your feet; and my sheep fed on what had been trampled by your feet, and drank what your feet had fouled. Therefore thus says the Lord God to them: Behold, I myself judge between fat cattle and lean (or between strong cattle and weak): because you thrust with your sides and shoulders and tossed all the weak cattle with your horns, until they were scattered abroad, I will save my flock and it shall no longer be a prey, and I will judge between cattle and cattle (or between ram and ram). And I will raise up over them (or them) one shepherd to feed them (or them), my servant David, he shall feed them (or them), and he shall be to them for a shepherd. But I the Lord will be to them for God, and my servant David prince in the midst of them: I the Lord have spoken. And I will make with them a covenant (or testament) of peace, and I will make the most evil beasts cease from the land, and those who dwelt in the desert shall sleep secure in the woods; and I will make them, round about my hill, a blessing, and I will bring down (or give) the rain in its season: there shall be rains of blessing. And the tree of the field shall give (or the trees of the plains shall give) its fruit, and the earth shall give its shoot (or strength), and they shall be (or dwell) in their own land without fear (or in hope of peace), and they shall know that I am the Lord, when I have broken the chains (or the collar) of their yoke, and rescued them from the hand of those who ruled over them (or who made them serve). And they shall no longer be a prey to the nations, nor shall the beasts of the earth devour them, but they shall dwell confidently (or in hope) without any terror. And I will raise up for them a renowned shoot (or a planting of peace), and they shall no longer be diminished (or perishing) by famine in the land, nor shall they bear any longer the reproaches of the nations; and they shall know that I am the Lord their God with them, and they my people, the house of Israel, says the Lord God. But you, my flocks, the flocks of my pasture (or sheep), are men, and I the Lord your God, says the Lord God. I have often pointed out that I mix the two editions so as to avoid making the books too large, at least in those places that do not differ much from each other in translation. After Jerusalem was taken, after the one who had escaped brought the news to Babylon, he spoke concerning those who dwelt in the ruins of Jerusalem, and then to those who, though placed in captivity, nonetheless persevered in wickedness, unwilling to hear the prophet's words; now he directs his discourse to the shepherds, that is, to the princes, by whose fault the sheep, that is, the peoples, were scattered. And this must be noted, that from the twelfth year, the tenth month, the fifth of the month of the exile — or of the captivity of Jeconiah and of those who had been taken captive with him —, up to the twenty-fifth year, when the temple is built upon the mountain of the built city and the incredible mysteries of the Church are laid open, no year and no time is set in between, but it is simply said: 'The word of the Lord came to me, saying: Speak to these and to those', so that we should understand that all the things read over thirteen years, though spoken at different times, nevertheless do not have fixed intervals of time between them. But the discourse is directed to the shepherds of Israel — whom we ought to take either as the kings and princes, the scribes and Pharisees and the teachers of the Jewish people, or certainly, in the people of the Gospel, as the bishops, presbyters and deacons, or, according to the mystical senses, as the angels of the individual churches, to whom John writes in his Revelation, and whose angels daily see the face of God —, and first it is said: Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who, when they ought to feed the Lord's flock and provide for its welfare, hasten after their own luxury — whence great care must be taken, and those precepts observed: Do not seek to become a judge, lest perhaps you be unable to take away iniquities, and again: The greater you are, the more humble yourself, and you will find grace in the sight of the Lord, and once more: Have they made you leader? Do not be lifted up: be among them as one of them; whence the Apostle too says that he was among the disciples as a little one and a suckling —.

Quite clearly he states that they have caused the sheep to be lost and to be devoured by the beasts of the field; nor, if they are abandoned, could they avoid being lost in death and devoured. But he does not say that they should be restored after they have been lost in death and devoured.

But those pastors who did not care for the sheep, those were hirelings who used to feed themselves alone. On this account the Prophet addresses them, saying to them:—O ye pastors who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture, hear the word of the Lord. Thus saith the Lord: Lo! I will visit My sheep as the pastor visits his flock in the day of the whirlwind, and I will require My sheep at your hands. O foolish pastors, with the wool of the sheep do ye clothe yourselves and the flesh of the fatlings do eat, and the sheep ye do not feed. That which was sick ye did not heal, and that which was broken ye did not bind. The weak ye did not strengthen, and the lost and the scattered ye did not gather together. The strong ones and the fatlings ye did guard, but with harshness ye subdued them. The good pastures ye yourselves graze upon, and what remains ye trample with your feet. The pleasant waters do ye drink, and whatever remains ye defile with your feet. And My sheep have eaten the trampled (herbage) which your feet have trampled, and they have drunk the waters which your feet have defiled. These are the greedy and base pastors and hirelings, who did not feed the sheep, or guide them well, or deliver them from the wolves. But when the Great Pastor, the chief of pastors, shall come, He will call and visit His sheep and will take knowledge of His flock. And He will bring forward those pastors, and will exact an account from them, and will condemn them for their deeds. And those who fed the sheep well, them the Chief of Pastors will cause to rejoice and to inherit life and rest.

For you must know, and not be in doubt, that while before your election you lived to yourself, after it, you live for your flock. And before you had received the grace of the episcopate, no one knew you; but after you became one, the laity expect you to bring them food, namely instruction from the Scriptures. When then they expect, and suffer hunger, and you are feeding yourself only, and our Lord Jesus Christ comes and we stand before Him, what defence will you offer when He sees His own sheep hungering? For had you not taken the money, He would not have blamed you. But He would reasonably do so if upon taking it you dug and buried it,—in the words which God forbid that your piety should ever hear: ‘Thou oughtest to have given my money to the bankers, that when I came I might demand it of them.’

You see, we whom the Lord has deigned, thanks to no merits of ours, to set in this high station (about which a very strict account indeed has to be rendered) have two things about us that must be clearly distinguished: one, that we are Christians, the other, that we are placed in charge. Being Christians is for our sake; being in charge is for yours. It is to our advantage that we are Christians, only to yours that we are in charge.

Let him use those tenths and first-fruits, which are given according to the command of God, as a man of God; as also let him dispense in a right manner the free-will offerings which are brought in on account of the poor, to the orphans, the widows, the afflicted, and strangers in distress, as having that God for the examiner of his accounts who has committed the disposition to him. Distribute to all those in want with righteousness, and yourselves use the things which belong to the Lord, but do not abuse them; eating of them, but not eating them all up by yourselves: communicate with those that are in want, and thereby show yourselves unblameable before God. For if you shall consume them by yourselves, you will be reproached by God, who says to such unsatiable people, who alone devour all, "You eat up the milk, and clothe yourselves with the wool;" [Ezekiel 34:3] and in another passage, "Must you alone live upon the earth"? [Isaiah 5:8] Upon which account you are commanded in the law, "You shall love your neighbour as yourself." [Leviticus 19:18] Now we say these things, not as if you might not partake of the fruits of your labours; for it is written, "You shall not muzzle the mouth of the ox which treads out the grain;" [Deuteronomy 25:4; 1 Corinthians 9:9] but that you should do it with moderation and righteousness. As, therefore, the ox that labours in the threshing-floor without a muzzle eats indeed, but does not eat all up; so do you who labour in the threshing-floor, that is, in the Church of God, eat of the Church: which was also the case of the Levites, who served in the tabernacle of the testimony, which was in all things a type of the Church.

As for what follows: You ate the milk and covered yourselves with the wool, it is by a μεταφορὰν [metaphor] of shepherds that he speaks to the princes — of whom it is also written in another place: Who devour my people like a meal of bread —; in the milk understand all wealth, in the wool the manifold variety of garments. And what is said: And what was fat you slaughtered, speaks of the rich of the people, whom the wicked princes in the churches are said to slaughter, in that they praise them and dare not rebuke their vices — of whom the prophet also says: My people, those who call you blessed lead you astray, and trip up the path of your feet; of whom James too speaks, saying that when they have come in to them, clothed in costly garments and with a gold ring, they are honored by them, and to the holy poor it is said: But you, sit on the footstool, or on the ground, or stand there — what is weak they do not strengthen or make firm — whence Paul says: Receive the weak, and: Take up the one weak in faith, and: Many weak among you and sick, to whom is sent the divine word of which it is written in the Psalms: He sent his word and healed them, and rescued them from their corruptions —; 'and what is broken', he says, 'they do not bind up', by no means taking account of the mortal wounds among the peoples, such as the adulterer, the murderer, the sacrilegious man; 'and what is cast off, or what they see straying, they do not bring back', allowing them to be deceived by heretics; 'and what has perished they do not seek', desiring not so much to save the lost as to devour those who are in the churches, but ruling over them with harshness and with power — which properly pertains to the haughtiness of bishops, namely of those who disgrace the dignity of their name by their works and take up pride in place of humility, so that they think they have attained an honor, not a burden, and whomever they see in the church taking the lead and possessing the word of God, they strive to oppress; whence according to the Seventy it is written: And what was strong you afflicted with toil —.

In the same way, everyone who leads a bad life for all those to see whom he has been put in charge of, as far as he is concerned is killing even the strong ones. Any who imitate him die; whoever does not imitate him lives.

Hasten then to increase the flock of your master! Do not turn aside to relaxations or pleasures of the body or vilely squander the wool and the fat of Christ's sheep by hoarding up the goods of the monastery for your own benefit rather than of the brothers, so that you may enjoy yourself. Do nothing whatever, do not say anything for the sake of human glory, that does not pertain to the good of your monastery.

And since it is incumbent on us who seem to be in charge and in the place of shepherds to guard the flock, if we should be found negligent, what will be said to us was said to our predecessors who were such negligent leaders.

If we scorn the repentance of those who have in some degree the assurance of a bearable conscience, immediately they are drawn by the devil's invitation into heresy or schism with their wife and children, whom they had kept unharmed. And it will be charged against us on judgment day that we have not cared for the wounded sheep and have lost many innocent ones because of one wounded.

Do you see a shepherd's vigilance? Do you see his heightened interest? What excuse could they have to whom rational flocks are entrusted but who are guilty of great negligence and day after day, in the prophet's words, slaughter some of them and look on without intending to take any care of others made the prey of wild beasts or the spoils of other people—even when the labor involved is slight and attention easy? It is a soul, after all, that is to be instructed; but that involves much labor for body and soul.

Having therefore mentioned the marks of a shepherd, Christ hath put two kinds of spoilers; one, the thief who kills and steals; the other, one who doth not these things, but who when they are done doth not give heed nor hinder them. By the first, pointing to Theudas and those like him; by the second, exposing the teachers of the Jews, who neither cared for nor thought about the sheep entrusted to them. On which account Ezekiel of old rebuked them, and said, "Woe, ye shepherds of Israel! Do the shepherds feed themselves? Do not the shepherds feed the sheep?" But they did the contrary, which is the worst kind of wickedness, and the cause of all the rest. Wherefore It saith, "They have not turned back the strayed, nor sought the lost, nor bound up the broken, nor healed the sick, because they fed themselves and not the sheep."... From both Christ distinguisheth Himself; from those who came to spoil, by saying, "I am come that they might have life, and that they might have more abundantly"; and from those who cared not for the sheep being carried away by wolves, by never deserting them, but even laying down His life for them, that the sheep might not perish.
Homily on the Gospel of John 60

As regards the feeble it is to be feared that some trial may happen to him and break him. But the sick person is already ill with some kind of greed and prevented by some kind of greed from entering on the way of God, from submitting to the yoke of Christ. Think of people who want to lead a good life, who are already determined to lead a good life and are less capable of enduring evil, while they are quite ready to do good. But it is part of a Christian's strength not only to do what is good but also to put up with what is bad.
The shepherds who feed themselves and not the sheep are being told what they are diligent about and what they are negligent about.

If I do not worry about the one that strays and gets lost, even the one that is strong will think it is rather fun to stray and get lost. I do indeed desire outward gains, but I am more afraid of inner losses.

Since we have been appointed by the Lord to direct the ship of his church, let us with his help and the direction of the two Testaments so govern the ship of his church that we may not through some negligence turn aside either to the right or to the left but may without effort keep a straight course of life in the midst of the great dangers of this world. Just as any ship cannot gather earthly profits without many labors, so the ship of the church cannot obtain the gains and joy of the eternal homeland without many tribulations. For just as pilots of ships, if they fail to be alert because of an excessive desire for sleep or false sense of security and do not show the sailors what they should do, immediately suffer shipwreck, so unless the church's pilots with all vigilance teach, terrify, sometimes even censure and occasionally punish lightly, at times even threatening the day of judgment with severity and thus showing how to keep the straight path of eternal life, it is to be feared that they will receive judgment where they might have had a remedy. For this reason, with the inspiration and assistance of the Lord, let us endeavor as far as it lies in our power to inform by word and example the people entrusted to our care.

It is the abbot's responsibility to have great concern and to act with all speed, discernment and diligence in order not to lose any of the sheep entrusted to him. He should realize that he has undertaken care of the sick, not tyranny over the healthy.

For one who had been cast away is brought back, when any one who has fallen into sin is recalled to a state of righteousness by the vigour of pastoral solicitude. For ligature binds a fracture when discipline subdues a sin, lest the wound should bleed mortally for want of being compressed by the severity of constraint. But often a fracture is made worse, when it is bound together unwarily, so that the cut is more severely felt from being immoderately constrained by ligaments. Hence it is needful that when a wound of sin in subordinates is repressed by correction, even constraint should moderate itself with great carefulness, to the end that it may so exercise the rights of discipline against delinquents as to retain the bowels of loving-kindness.

Let us struggle, my beloved, during these six days of the Passover, for they are given to us each year for the redemption of our souls, that we may spend them in the works of God.… He sent to us the great Shepherd of the sheep that were scattered, to gather us back into his holy fold.

And the people of God was scattered, either by vices or by heretical error, because there was no good shepherd who would lay down his life for the sheep, but all were hirelings, who consider only the profits from the flocks and flee when they see the wolf; through whose negligence the Lord's flock is devoured by the beasts of the field — of which it is written: You set darkness, and night came: in it all the beasts of the field will pass through, the lions' whelps roaring, to seize and to seek their food from God —.

And they are scattered, and they wander on all the mountains, who are lifted up against the knowledge of God, and on every high hill, who through heretical pride despise the simplicity of the Church, and they are scattered over the whole face of the earth, seeking earthly things, not heavenly: And there was none who would seek, nor who would bring back, because, occupied with their pleasures, they do not care about the losses of the Lord's flock.

Pursuing all earthly objects, things that glitter obviously on the face of the earth, they love them, they set their hearts on them. They do not want to die, that their life may be hidden with Christ.… Not all heretics are to be found all over the face of the earth, but still heretics are to be found all over the face of the earth. Some here, others there, but there is no lack of them anywhere.

Hence the word of the Lord comes to the wicked shepherds, 'because you have done this and that', the things which I expounded above and which he enumerates a second time. 'Behold, I myself will come to the shepherds and will require my flock at their hand, for whom it is better that a donkey's millstone be tied to their neck than that they scandalize the least of my people; and this will be their punishment, even the greatest: That they no longer feed my flock, lest, under the pretext of the sheep, they feed themselves and amass wealth; and I will deliver my people from their mouth'.

But which shepherds are dead? Those who seek their own advantage, not that of Jesus Christ. So will there be shepherds, and will they be found, who do not seek their own advantage but that of Jesus Christ? There certainly will be, and they will certainly be found; they are not lacking, and they won't be lacking. So let us see what the Lord has to say, who says he lives; whether he says he is going to take the sheep away from the bad shepherds, who feed themselves, not the sheep, and give them to good shepherds, who feed the sheep, not themselves.

These words predict the end both of the kingdom of the Jews and the priesthood. I will free my flocks, he says, from those who look after them badly, who have steered them with no kind of providence but have only continued to devour them. Therefore through our Lord and Savior they are granted salvation.

'I will require', he says, 'from the hand', and 'I will deliver from the mouth', by which they are devoured with greedy jaws; and when he has sought out the sheep, he visits them as sick and lean and scattered through the negligence of the shepherds; and he will deliver them from all places in the day of cloud and gloom — of which Joel too speaks: The day of the Lord is at hand, and it is near; a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and mist —.

Listen and learn, you sheep of God; from the bad shepherds God will require his sheep, and from their hands he will require their death.… So let us see, because that is what I had proposed to do, whether he takes the sheep away from the bad shepherds and gives them to good shepherds.

Rain and fog, the errors of this world; a great darkness arising from human lusts, a thick fog covering the earth. And it is difficult for the sheep not to go astray in this fog. But the shepherd does not desert them. He seeks them, his piercing gaze penetrates the fog, the thick darkness of the clouds does not prevent him.
He is shepherd to shepherds and a guide to guides: that we may feed his flock with knowledge, not with the instruments of a foolish shepherd.
IN DEFENSE OF HIS FLIGHT TO PONTUS, ORATION 2:117
When it is difficult for them to be found, now I will find them. The fog is dense, the storm cloud thick; nothing escapes his eyes.

Then they are led out from the lands, so as to be brought into their own land, which is the land of the living, and so that he himself may feed them on the mountains of Israel — of which David speaks: I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, whence help will come to me —, and not only on the mountains, but by the streams and in all the dwelling places of the land, in the richest pastures and on the high mountain — of which Isaiah and Micah prophesy more fully —, or on the high mountains, Israel; there they will rest in green grass — and they will say: The Lord feeds me, and nothing will be lacking to me: in a place of pasture, there he has set me; beside the water of refreshment he has brought me up —, and they will feed in the fattest pastures upon the mountains of Israel.

He established the mountains of Israel, the authors of the divine Scriptures. Feed there, in order to feed without a qualm. Whatever you hear from that source, let that taste good to you; anything from outside, spit it out. In order not to go astray in the fog, listen to the voice of the Shepherd. Gather yourselves to the mountains of holy Scripture. There you will find your heart's desire, there is nothing poisonous there, nothing unsuitable; they are the richest pastures.

There, life is wisdom, through which all these things come into being, both those that have been and those that will be. Yet, it is not made but is as it was, and thus it will be forever. Or rather, to have been in the past or to be in the future does not pertain to it, but simply to be, for it is eternal. To be in the past or to be in the future is not to be eternal.
This is feeding Christ, this is feeding for Christ, this is feeding in Christ, not feeding oneself apart from Christ. There is not really a dearth of shepherds.

And it is an infinite promise and a hope of blessedness, when the Lord himself promises, saying: 'I will feed my sheep, and I will by no means entrust them to wicked shepherds, and I will make them lie down, says the Lord God, so that they may rest in the bosom of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob'.
Lift up your eyes to the mountains, by all means, from where help shall come to you—but pay attention to him saying, I myself will be the shepherd.

O shepherds, disciples of the Lord, feed the flock and lead (it) well! Strengthen the sick, support the weak, bind up the broken, make whole the lame, and take heed to the fattened ones for the Lord of the flock. Be not likened unto an unskilled and foolish shepherd, who in his foolishness is not able to feed the flock, and whose arm is dried up, and whose eye has been blinded, because he said: "dying, let it die; and perishing, let it perish, and the flesh that is left shall be eaten by its companions ". And when the Chief of the shepherds comes He will condemn the unskilled and foolish shepherd who has not cared well for his fellow servants. And he who has shepherded the flock and led (it) well shall be called "a good and skillful servant" (cf. S. Mt. 25: 21), who has presented the flock to the Shepherd while it was intact.

If you are a shepherd, take care that none of your pastoral duties is neglected. And what are these duties? To bring back that which is lost, to bind up that which was broken, to heal that which is diseased.
HOMILY ON THE WORDS 'GIVE HEED TO THYSELF.'

Then what had perished among the peoples of the nations will be sought, and what had strayed through the persuasion of heretics will be brought back, and what had been broken will be bound up, and what is crushed and weak will be made firm — that what is written may be fulfilled: Who heals their infirmities, and binds up their bruises. A heart, indeed, crushed and humbled, God does not spurn; whence the holy man too says: Heal me, for my bones are troubled, and in Psalm 37 (38), repenting: There is no peace, he says, for my bones before the face of my sins —. And what will be fat, he says, and strong I will guard, lest it be devoured by beasts; and he will feed his sheep in judgment, knowing what pastures are owed to which sheep — for Diverse indeed are the dwellings with the Father. And the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son —. These things, then, he spoke against the shepherds.

The Lord did not say, "I will provide other good shepherds to do these things," but "I myself," he said, "will do them. I will commit my sheep to nobody else." You are all right, brothers; you are all right, you sheep. It is we bishops, it seems, who have got to worry, there being apparently not a single good shepherd.

The words against the false shepherds have been hidden, as well as the prediction of God's attentiveness to come. He turns his words to the flocks and teaches the useless shepherds how not to fall back in any way in defending them.
In every good deed we are anticipated by the Lord's grace. He deigns to inspire us to make us wish to entreat him.

But surely if we neglect our duties, does Almighty God abandon His sheep? By no means; for He Himself, as He promised through the prophet, feeds them by Himself, and He instructs all whom He has predestined to life through the goads of afflictions and the spirit of compunction.

We must all of us strive zealously to make known to the church both the dreadfulness of the coming judgment and the kingdom of heaven's delight. Those who are not in a position to address a large assembly should instruct individuals, offering instruction in personal talks; they should try to serve those around them through simple encouragement.… You who are pastors, consider that you are pasturing God's flock. We often see a block of salt put out for animals to lick for their well-being. Priests among their people should be like blocks of salt. They should counsel everyone in their flocks in such a way that all those with whom they come in contact may be seasoned with eternal life as if they had been sprinkled with salt. We who preach are not the salt of the earth unless we season the hearts of those who listen to us. We are really preaching to others if we ourselves do what we say, if we are pierced with God's love, if, since we cannot avoid sin, our tears wash away the stains on our life that come with each new day. We truly feel remorse when we take to heart the lives of our forebears in the faith so that we are diminished in our own eyes. Then do we truly feel remorse, when we attentively examine God's teachings and adopt for our own use what those we revere themselves used for theirs. And while we are moved to remorse on our own account, let us also take responsibility for the lives of those entrusted to our care. Our own bitter compunction should not divert us from concern for our neighbor. What good to love and strive to do good for our neighbor and abandon ourselves? We must realize that our passion for justice in the face of another's evil must never cause us to lose the virtue of gentleness. Priests must not be quick-tempered or rash; they must instead be temperate and thoughtful. We must support those we challenge and challenge those we support. If we neglect this, our work will lack either courage or gentleness. What shall we call the human soul but the food of the Lord? It is created to become nothing less than Christ's body and to bring about growth in the eternal church. We priests are to season this food. Cease to pray, cease to teach, and the salt loses its taste.

We who desire to be flocks of the shepherd must never try to escape from being fed even by the very things that seem to diverge from Scripture and are trampled on because of the discordance of what is said by those who neither want nor can use the nourishment that Scripture gives in all its fullness.

Now he speaks to the sheep, that is, to the people, and to the flock of both kinds of cattle, that is, of sheep and of goats, and not only to the sheep and goats, but to the rams and he-goats, who are the princes in the flocks; to whom he says: 'Was it not enough for you that you fed on the good pastures of the Scriptures? But on top of that you will trample the remnants of your pastures with your feet, and when you drank the purest water of God's utterances, you fouled the rest of the waters with your feet, so that my people ate the pastures trampled by you and drank the fouled waters, and, through your fault, received corrupted and violated what was good in itself'. This indeed all heretics do, picking at the utterances of the Scriptures and, as far as in them lies, staining them; but churchmen who do not guard the truth of doctrines, but fabricate them from their own heart and have their own presumption for their teacher, are held fast in a like error; who, when they have persuaded the people that what they fabricate is true, and have stirred up applause and shouts in the manner of the theater, become forgetful of their own lack of skill, and, with brow drawn up and with words weighed and balanced, assume for themselves the authority of teachers.
If you really think, brothers, what a very great blessing it is to be God's flock, you must be filled even in the midst of these tears and troubles of ours with very great joy.

What are he-goats doing here in God's flock? In the same pastures, at the same springs, he-goats, though destined for the left hand, are mixing with those of the right hand, and those who are going to be separated are first tolerated. And this is to exercise the sheep in a patience after the likeness of God's own patience.

I am judging. What a relief, what reassurance! [The Lord] is judging; the good can be reassured. No opponent can corrupt their judge, no counselor twist him round their little finger or witness play fast and loose with him. But just as the good can be reassured, so to the same extent the bad should be afraid. He is not the sort of judge things can be kept hidden from. Do you imagine, after all, that God as judge is going to examine witnesses, to learn from them who you may be? How can he possibly be mistaken about who you may be, seeing that he knew what you were going to be?
God's pastures are good, and God's springs are pure. We have them in the holy Scriptures.

For indeed the shepherds drink most pure water, when with a right understanding they imbibe the streams of truth. But to foul the same water with their feet is to corrupt the studies of holy meditation by evil living. And verily the sheep drink the water fouled by their feet, when any of those subject to them follow not the words which they hear, but only imitate the bad examples which they see. Thirsting for the things said, but perverted by the works observed, they take in mud with their draughts, as from polluted fountains.

Let us see, then, what the judgment between cattle and cattle is, and with what judgment the good and true shepherd judges them, he who received all judgment from the Father: Behold, he says, I myself judge between fat cattle and lean (or between strong and weak): for the strong thrust with their sides and shoulders and dash against the weak cattle and toss them with their horns, not knowing that in the law the goring bull must be punished; and they thrust with their sides and tossed with their horns until they scattered the sheep and drove them out: for through the pride of the greater and the iniquity of those set over them, they are frequently driven from the church, so that those whom the Lord himself saved are scattered away from him; but the Lord will no longer abandon them to be a prey, and he will judge between cattle and cattle: not between the names of dignities with which those set over others swell, but between man and man, according as each is a servant of the Lord.
He makes no further mention of the he-goats. He mentioned them once, so that we would know they exist. He knows them well. After that he speaks as if all are sheep.

If we lament the many sheep that are straying outside, woe to those whose shoulders and sides and horns have brought it about. It is only strong sheep who would do this. Who are the strong? Those who rely on their own righteousness. None but those who called themselves just divided the sheep and drove them outside. Shoulders bold at shoving, because they do not bear God's burden; evil sides, conspiracies of friends, companions in obstinacy; horns lifted up, high and mighty pride. Shove with sides and shoulders, flail with your horns, drive outside what you have not bought. Certainly this is your whole case, that you are just and others are unjust, and it was unfitting that the just should remain with the unjust, unfitting, that is to say, that the corn should remain among the weeds, unfitting that the sheep should feed among the goats until the shepherd should come who would make no mistake in separating them.

Just as we must abominate their injustice and cruelty, so we must praise the mercy of our Shepherd, who is truly our God; he will save his sheep. Perhaps, my brothers, he is doing this when we say this, doing it through the least of his servants, doing it perhaps through unworthy servants. Let him save his sheep; let them hear the voice of their Shepherd and follow him. Do not let them look for a proof of the church from the mouth of people. Let them look for it from the mouth of God, look for it from the mouth of Christ. Whoever he calls ungodly is ungodly, whoever he calls just is just, whoever he calls a sheep is a sheep, whoever he calls a goat is a goat. He himself is truth, let him speak, let the church be sought from him. Tell us, Lord, where is your church?

David also is called the Christ, as when Ezekiel prophesied to the shepherds and added, in the person of God, "I will raise up David my servant, who will shepherd them." For the patriarch David will not be raised up to shepherd the saints, but Christ.
COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 1:146

On this principle again all the kings whom they had in honor after his time were named from him, both by the people themselves and by God. For both Ezekiel and other prophets besides speak of David as coming and rising again; not meaning him that was dead, but them who were emulating his virtue. And to Hezekiah He saith, "I will defend this city, for mine own sake and for my servant David's sake."
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 2:6

Hence also in the same Ezekiel it is written: I will raise up over them one shepherd, and he shall feed them, my servant David; and he shall be their shepherd, and I the Lord will be their God, and David a prince in their midst. I the Lord have spoken, and I will make with David a covenant of peace (Ezek 34:23-25).
